papers.title: Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae sp. nov. isolated from a septic immunocompromised patient in Brazil
papers.abstract: Pannonibacter species. are non-fermentative Gram-stain-negative bacteria, with rare reports of human infections primarily affecting immunocompromised patients. Here, we report the genomic and phenotypic characterization of a novel Pannonibacter species, isolated from a bacteremia episode in a pediatric patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in Brazil. Initial characterization of the isolate (here named CBAS 1226) by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing identified it as Pannonibacter sp., most closely related to P. phragmitetus. However, comparison of its MALDI-TOF spectrum with a commercial reference library revealed compatibility with only two of the five main spectra profiles for P. phragmitetus. This discrepancy motivated comprehensive genomic, biochemical, morphological, and antimicrobial resistance profiling of CBAS 1226. Genomic analysis revealed that Pannonibacter sp. CBAS 1226 is phylogenetically distinct from P. phragmitetus and other known species, with ANI and dDDH values below species delineation thresholds, supporting its proposal as Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae. It forms small, non-hemolytic, grayish-white colonies on blood agar, similar to its closest relatives P. phragmitetus and P. indicus. Phenotypically, it is distinguished by positive - and {beta}-glucosidase activity, along with the utilization of citrate, L-proline, and 2-ketoglutarate. It is negative for alkaline phosphatase and unable to utilize D-fructose, D-melibiose, esculin, or L-arginine. The isolate exhibited higher MICs for {beta}-lactams, whereas carbapenems and fluoroquinolones showed low MICs. The isolate is capable of forming biofilms and tolerates alkaline conditions, a wide range of temperatures, and different oxygen concentrations. Altogether, this report emphasizes the relevance of additional proteomics- and genomics-based approaches to clarify unusual bacterial infections and describes a new Pannonibacter species with distinct features and the potential to cause opportunistic infections.

papers.title: Cryo-EM Structure of Mycobacteriophage D29 Reveals a Specialized Portal-Capsid Junction and a Unique 13-Subunit Baseplate Collar
papers.abstract: Mycobacteriophages are promising agents against drug-resistant mycobacterial infections, yet their structural organization and host-recognition mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we determined cryo-EM structures of the capsid, connector, tail tube, and baseplate of the lytic, broad-host-range mycobacteriophage D29, revealing a near-complete virion architecture. At the capsid-portal interface, five copies of the previously uncharacterized protein gp19.1 bridge adjacent capsid subunits around the dodecameric portal, potentially reinforcing the symmetry-mismatched vertex. At the baseplate, 13 copies of gp6 assemble into a collar surrounding the sixfold-symmetric gp23-gp27 core. Remarkably, this 6:13 symmetry mismatch is accommodated through six distinct gp6- gp27 interfaces involving 12 gp6 subunits, leaving one subunit largely disengaged from the core. This asymmetric organization produces a tilted, outward-flaring collar that presents an extensive surface with the potential to engage the host cell. Whole-cell binding and plaque-competition assays further implicate the gp6 collar and the flexible trimeric central fiber gp31 in host recognition. Together, these findings reveal distinct structural adaptations at symmetry-mismatched interfaces and provide a structural framework for understanding mycobacteriophage assembly and host engagement.

papers.title: Ultra-small bacteria and their phages discovered through metagenomics in a sub-arctic degrading permafrost ecosystem
papers.abstract: Patescibacteriota is a diverse bacterial phylum characterized by ultra-small cell size, streamlined genome, incomplete metabolism and episymbiotic lifestyle. While Patescibacteriota have been detected across a wide range of ecosystem types, their phages are not widely described. We utilized metagenomics to explore these less characterized parts of the microbiome in a sporadic permafrost ecosystem, with samples from palsa and peat soils, small ponds and streams. We retrieved 33 high-quality metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) of Patescibacteriota, mainly from the classes Minisyncoccia and Saccharimonadia. Minisyncoccia was a dominant class in the thawing soils and thaw ponds, whereas the Saccharimonadia was more abundant in the frozen palsa soil layers. The distribution of the Patescibacteria classes was also reflected in their metabolic potential. For example, gluconeogenesis pathway was complete only in MAGs from the class Minisyncoccia, whereas cytochrome o ubiquinol oxidase was mainly found from the MAGs of the class Saccharimondia. The viral community analysis yielded 16 354 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), which represented mainly tailed dsDNA viruses from the class Caudoviricetes. Based on genome size, 16 vOTUs were qualified as jumbophages and one as a megaphage. Similar to the bacterial community, the viral community composition differed across sample types. The most common hosts for bacterial viruses were phyla Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Actinomycetota. A further 196 vOTUs were in silico linked to Patescibacteriota hosts. The Patescibacteriota phages were diverse, with only two vOTUs representing the same genus. The relative abundance of Patescibacteriota-associated phages was especially high in frozen palsa soils, largely following the same pattern of abundance as Patescibacteriota.

papers.title: Virucidal Star Polymer Disrupts Alphavirus Infection in Aedes Mosquitoes
papers.abstract: Mosquito-borne alphaviruses represent an increasing global health threat, yet there are currently no antiviral interventions capable of targeting both the vertebrate host and mosquito vector. Here, we investigated the antiviral potential of the heparan sulfate proteoglycan-mimicking zwitterionic polymer ZP12 against alphavirus infection in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. ZP12 exhibited potent antiviral and virucidal activity against Ross River virus (RRV) and Semliki Forest virus (SFV) in C6/36 mosquito cells. Antiviral activity was retained in ex vivo mosquito gut cultures, where both high (100 g/mL) and low (0.5 g/mL) concentrations significantly reduced RRV replication, with viral titres reduced by up to five orders of magnitude at peak infection. Delayed-treatment studies demonstrated that ZP12 retained antiviral activity after infection had been initiated, although efficacy declined as treatment was delayed. To evaluate prophylactic delivery, mosquitoes were exposed to ZP12 through sugar feeding prior to viral challenge. While this approach did not directly protect against subsequent gut infection, follow-up experiments demonstrated that ZP12 remained biologically active within the mosquito, suggesting that limited delivery to the midgut rather than loss of antiviral activity restricted efficacy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ZP12 is a potent antiviral and virucidal agent against alphaviruses in mosquito cells and tissues and supports its further development as a transmission-blocking strategy for arboviral control.

papers.title: A Luciferase Reporter of Ester Prodrug Delivery to the Cytosol of Intracellular Mycobacteria
papers.abstract: The bacterial cell envelope restricts access to cytoplasmic targets and is a principal reason that otherwise potent antibacterial compounds fail in cells. Masking an anionic carboxylic acid as an ester is a common way to cross that barrier, but the strategy succeeds only if the target organism also hydrolyzes the ester once the compound arrives. These two requirements, permeation and intracellular unmasking, are rarely measured together in live bacterial cells, and existing reporters cannot specify where unmasking occurred. Here we describe a bioluminescent platform that resolves both steps in real time in live mycobacteria using carboxylate esters of D-luciferin. Luciferase requires that an ester both reach the bacterial cytoplasm and be hydrolyzed there, which makes light a compartment-specific readout of productive delivery. Across a series of alkyl esters in Mycobacterium smegmatis, chain length governed permeation while branching adjacent to the carbonyl governed esterase processing, indicating that the two parameters can be tuned independently. The n-butyl ester gave the strongest signal in broth, in infected macrophages, and in the pathogen Mycobacterium avium, whereas the tert-butyl ester was inert in Mycobacterium avium and unmasking of the whole series was attenuated at phagosomal pH. Ester activation is therefore both species- and compartment-dependent, and masking groups are best selected in the organism and environment in which they must act.

papers.title: Strain-specific early, host-shaped late: the rhizobial transcriptome across symbiosis
papers.abstract: The two ends of the rhizobial symbiotic trajectory have only been described separately. Here we report strand-specific RNA-seq of bacteroids of two strains, each against free-living cells of the same strain and alongside its flavonoid response: Sinorhizobium fredii HH103 from soybean (Glycine max), Glycyrrhiza uralensis and Lotus burttii, and Rhizobium tropici CIAT 899 from common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and L. burttii, the one legume both strains nodulate. Between 1877 and 2284 genes respond per strain-host combination, and most of that response is host-common: 1171 of 2855 genes respond in all three hosts of HH103 and 1664 of 2703 in both hosts of CIAT 899. What distinguishes the remainder is host identity rather than nodule type, since HH103 bacteroids from the indeterminate-nodule G. uralensis resemble those from L. burttii more than either resembles those from soybean, its natural host. Nitrogen fixation and the stress response are over-represented in every bacteroid and motility is almost entirely repressed, yet the shared core of CIAT 899 is the only repression-dominated gene set here and its translational machinery is induced where that of HH103 is repressed. Dismantling of the early programme is selective: in HH103 the type III apparatus is switched off, the Nod factor operons are attenuated but retained, and the fixABCX operon under a nod box is amplified, so a nod box does not by itself mark a gene as early. CIAT 899, lacking a type III system and placing no nif/fix gene under flavonoid control, keeps that block flat until the nodule, then engages 26 of its 30 genes. Across genera, 26% of responding orthologue pairs are shared in the bacteroid against 5% in the flavonoid response: each bacterium negotiates entry in a dialect of its own and converges on a shared end state whose amplitude, rather than content, the host modulates.

papers.title: Flexible phosphorus allocation to the phosphoproteome underpins diatom regulatory adaptations to fluctuating phosphate supply
papers.abstract: Diatoms are major drivers of marine phosphorus (P) cycling and are highly adapted to cope with variable P supply. P-starved diatoms can sense increases in P availability within seconds, accumulating this limiting resource through luxury polyphosphate (polyP) storage. Yet, how diatoms coordinate such responses is unknown. Protein phosphorylation is a core mechanism for environmental signal transduction in eukaryotes, but how cells balance investment in protein phosphorylation against competing physiological demands during P limitation is poorly understood. Here, we characterise system-wide remodelling of the Phaeodactylum tricornutum phosphoproteome in response to P deficiency and subsequent resupply. We identify widespread proteome dephosphorylation across 44% of phosphosites, revealing a previously unrecognised P-sparing strategy in marine phytoplankton. Following P resupply, diatoms orchestrate extensive phosphoproteome reprogramming within minutes. We characterise previously unrecognized components for early recovery from P limitation, including a novel environmentally prevalent intracellular H+/phosphate transporter strongly conserved in diverse diatoms. We also identify a vacuolar Ca2+-dependent protein kinase (CDPK) associated with polyP-storage granules. Mutant and inhibitor analyses demonstrate a role for Ca2+- and CDPK-signalling in the regulation of luxury polyP accumulation. Our findings reveal that recovery from P starvation is mediated by rapid phosphoregulatory control of intracellular P trafficking, organellar ATP generation coupled with luxury P storage, enabling diatoms to exploit newly available P and thrive in fluctuating P regimes. Collectively, our study uncovers the phosphoproteome as a flexible intracellular P reservoir and establishes mechanistic links between intracellular P budgeting, signalling and the marine P cycle.

papers.title: Infection-dependent antibiotic response phenotypes emerge during chronic airway adaptation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Objectives Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infections can persist for years despite intensive antibiotic therapy guided by standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing. While this technique captures the emergence of resistance, it does not reproduce many features of the infection environment, where adaptation acquired during chronic infection may alter bacterial responses to antibiotics in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing. Here we investigated antibiotic responses of longitudinal clinical isolates under standard laboratory conditions and in an airway epithelial infection model. Methods Six longitudinal pairs of P. aeruginosa isolates from people with cystic fibrosis were analysed. Changes in bacterial growth following exposure to tobramycin, ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin were quantified under standard laboratory conditions and compared with changes in bacterial burden after treatment measured in differentiated airway epithelial cultures maintained under air-liquid interface (ALI) conditions that reproduce key features of the airway infection environment. Representative phenotypes were visualized by confocal microscopy and interpreted in the context of available whole-genome sequencing data. Results Major resistance phenotypes identified by conventional susceptibility testing were largely reproduced in the ALI model. However, concordance between phenotypes observed under standard laboratory and ALI conditions differed between antibiotics. Several isolates classified as susceptible according to conventional susceptibility testing displayed substantial survival in the ALI model, and these discordant phenotypes were observed predominantly among those isolates recovered after prolonged airway persistence. Genomic analyses identified mutations associated with both classical resistance mechanisms and chronic adaptation. Conclusions Phenotypes observed under conventional laboratory conditions do not uniformly predict those observed in the ALI airway conditions. Discordant phenotypes were most apparent among chronically adapted isolates and varied between antibiotics, suggesting that adaptation acquired during chronic infection can alter antibiotic responses in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing.

papers.title: Coupling Complementary Pathways in a Bacterial Co-culture Enables 4-Aminophenol Removal during Paracetamol Degradation
papers.abstract: Pharmaceutical biodegradation can generate potentially toxic metabolites that persist after the parent compound has been removed, posing additional risks to aquatic environments. Microbial co-cultures offer a promising strategy to address this challenge by combining complementary metabolic capabilities to remove both pharmaceuticals and their harmful transformation products by coupling complementary degradation pathways. Here, we investigated a two-species co-culture combining the paracetamol-degrading bacterium Delftia P1 with Microbacterium lacus to enable subsequent 4-AP removal. While Delftia P1 efficiently degraded paracetamol, it accumulated 4-AP as a dead-end metabolite. M. lacus was selected to complement this metabolic limitation because its genome contains a homolog of sadB, a monooxygenase gene involved in 4-AP transformation. The relative abundance of the two strains strongly influenced 4-AP removal, with the highest efficiency achieved at a Delftia P1:M. lacus cell-density ratio of 1:100, corresponding to an OD600nm ratio of 1:10. At this ratio, the co-culture achieved complete removal of paracetamol and 4-AP within 6 and 24 h, respectively. Its capacity was tested in wastewater, where 100% of paracetamol were removed within 4 h and no accumulation of 4-AP was observed within 24 h. These findings demonstrate the potential of cocultivating bacteria with complementary metabolic capabilities to address both pharmaceutical contamination and transformation-product accumulation. Moreover, the highest 4-AP removal was achieved when M. lacus was present at a 100-fold higher cell density than Delftia P1, highlighting the importance of considering relative cell densities when designing co-cultures.

papers.title: Chemical warfare in the rice plant rhizosphere: Diverse Pseudomonas antagonize the green alga Chlamydomonas
papers.abstract: Algae and bacteria form dynamic partnerships that shape diverse ecosystems. The model green microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is often found in paddy rice fields, where the diversity and functional characteristics of its bacterial partners remain largely unexplored. Here, we isolated 12 bacterial strains from the rice rhizosphere and its surrounding soil. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequences revealed that eight isolates belong to the genus Pseudomonas. Three Pseudomonas rhizosphere strains exhibited antagonistic effects against C. reinhardtii, negatively impacting its growth, pigmentation and cell morphology. Close physical associations between the three antagonistic Pseudomonas strains and C. reinhardtii were observed in liquid cultures. Whole genome sequencing identified the antagonistic strains as Pseudomonas alloputida, Pseudomonas tohonis, and Pseudomonas asiatica. The three bacterial genomes encode several factors well-known for mediating chemical warfare. Notably, P. tohonis bears a gene cluster encoding the phenolic toxin, 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG). DAPG inhibits the growth and alters the cell morphology of C. reinhardtii. These findings expand our understanding of the diversity of bacterial partners associated with C. reinhardtii and highlight the role of Pseudomonas rice rhizosphere-associated bacteria as potent green algal antagonists. They harbor a reservoir of common functional traits that negatively influence green algal population dynamics.

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

papers.title: The absence of microbiome in germ-free mice exacerbates the pathogenicity of mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10
papers.abstract: Germ-free mice, which are devoid of microbiota, provide a powerful system to define the contribution of the microbiome to host responses during infection. Severe COVID-19 outcomes are associated with multiple comorbidities that are themselves characterized by microbiome dysbiosis; however, the causal role of the microbiota in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we use germ-free mouse models to evaluate the impact of the microbiome on disease severity following infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10. Comparison with conventionally housed mice revealed that the absence of the microbiome markedly exacerbates SARS-CoV-2-induced disease in both C57BL/6 and Swiss Webster backgrounds. Germ-free mice exhibited greater weight loss, impaired lung function, worsened pulmonary pathology, and pronounced alterations in circulating cytokine and chemokine profiles compared with conventional controls. These findings show that resident microbiota limit SARS-CoV-2 pathogenicity and establish germ-free COVID-19 models as a powerful platform to identify protective microbial taxa and microbiota-based interventions to reduce severe disease.

papers.title: Divergent methane production and microbial community responses to carbon enrichment in freshwater wetland sediments
papers.abstract: Methane (CH4) accumulation in wetland sediments reflects interactions among organic matter, sediment chemistry, and microbial communities. We combined depth-resolved field characterization across four wetland habitats in northern Israel with complementary incubations to examine methane accumulation and responses to labile-carbon enrichment. Sediment cores were characterized using Rock-Eval analysis, porewater chemistry, oxygen profiling at three sites, and mcrA amplicon sequencing. High CH4 concentrations occurred under contrasting conditions: Ein Nimfit (EN) contained approximately 12% total organic carbon and reached 2.1 mM CH4, whereas Ein Afek site EA2 contained approximately 5% carbon and accumulated 0.7-1.7 mM CH4. Both showed sulfate depletion, but EN exhibited pronounced sulfide accumulation, whereas EA2 showed greater dissolved iron and nutrient enrichment. Their classified methanogenic assemblages also differed. EA1 remained methane poor despite increasing carbon content with depth, while EA3 combined low carbon content and CH4 accumulation with detectable methanogens and lower methanogenic diversity. In a 36-day bottle experiments using sediments from two of the four wetland habitats, sucrose-amended EA3 exhibited a transient maximum of 18.8 mmol collected CH4 kg-1 wet sediment during Days 22-29, whereas EN reached its highest collected amount during Days 29-36. Methane proportions increased before the large output increase in EA3 but remained comparatively stable and high in EN. Soluble chemical oxygen demand trajectories and microbial community changes also differed. These findings identify distinct biogeochemical settings supporting methane accumulation and demonstrate methanogenic potential in low-CH4 sediment, emphasizing the complementary information provided by field profiles, microbial characterization, and exploratory enrichment experiments.

papers.title: Reverse Transcription Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification Combined with Lateral Flow Assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for Rapid Detection of the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus (BDBV) Outbreak Strain
papers.abstract: Making accurate diagnosis is a critical first step in patient management and control for emerging and re-emerging disease outbreaks. Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is a filovirus that causes Ebola disease, and the 2026 outbreak highlights the need for rapid diagnostic approaches that can be deployed in settings with limited laboratory infrastructure. Here, we developed a reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification-lateral flow assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for rapid detection of the 2026 BDBV outbreak strain. LAMP primers were designed based on the genome sequence of the 2026 outbreak strain, and the conservation of the primer binding sites among all available 2026 outbreak genomes was confirmed in silico. LAMP primers were evaluated for analytical specificity and sensitivity using in vitro-transcribed RNA (ivtRNA) from BDBV and other filoviruses, as well as RNA derived from arboviruses and mammalian cells. Amplification products were detected using a Chromatography-Printed Array Strip (C-PAS) lateral flow platform. The newly designed primers specifically detected the presence of BDBV RNA without nonspecific amplification of the other viral or cellular RNA samples tested. Consistent amplification was observed down to 103 copies per reaction. In addition, BDBV viral RNA was successfully amplified, and the amplification products were detected using C-PAS, with the total workflow being completed within 25 min. These findings demonstrate the analytical specificity and sensitivity of the developed RT-LAMP-LFA assay and its compatibility with rapid visual lateral flow detection, supporting its potential application as a point-of-care approach for BDBV detection.

papers.title: Prevalent Integration of both Xenotropic and Ecotropic Murine Leukemia Virus in the Human Genome of Xenografts
papers.abstract: Humanized mouse models are widely used in medical research to represent human conditions (1, 2), but their fidelity could be compromised by mouse-originated infections. However, their susceptibility to mouse pathogens are rarely questioned (3). Here we screened 1,619 publicly available genomic sequencing runs from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models for the integration of murine leukemia virus (MLV), a rodent retrovirus exists in the mouse genome as an endogenous retrovirus (4), within the human genome. We discovered substantial enrichment of human-MLV chimeric DNA in approximately 25% of them. Analyzing the human-MLV junctions, we found about 90% of them bearing the unmistakable hallmarks of retroviral integration, including the canonical MLV boundaries and the distinctive 4-bp target site duplications (5, 6). It was also assumed that mouse strains without the highly infectious Bxv1 provirus are safe from MLV contamination in xenografts (7, 8). However, we found many PDX models derived from Bxv1- strains, including the widely used NSG strain, are also contaminated by the supposedly rodent-specific ecotropic MLV (E-MLV). We further confirmed a complete E-MLV integrated into the human genome by both HiFi and sanger sequencing. Our discovery raises concerns that mouse-to-human retroviral transmission and integration is more common and less restrictive than previously appreciated. They support examination of MLV integration as a feature of humanized mouse models with implications on the fidelity of these models in recapitulating human cells and tissues. Our discovery also has underscored the importance of comprehensively inactivation of porcine endogenous retroviruses for the clinical application of xenotransplatation (9, 10).

papers.title: POM121 regulates lentiviral nuclear import in a capsid-host factor-dependent manner
papers.abstract: Lentiviruses such as human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) access the nuclear lumen through the nuclear pore complex (NPC), a process coordinated by the interactions between the viral capsid and nucleoporins (NUPs). Here, using unbiased proteomic screens, we identified several capsid-associated NUPs, including POM121. Depletion of POM121 impaired HIV-1 infection in multiple cell lines and in primary CD4+ T cells, whereas equine infectious anaemia virus (EIAV) infection was enhanced, indicating that POM121 effect is virus-specific. A cytoplasmic carboxy-terminal fragment of POM121, containing its FG-rich region inhibited HIV-1 and a broader range of lentiviruses. Analysis of HIV-1 capsid mutants showed that physical interaction with POM121 does not predict functional dependence, as capsids retaining POM121 binding remained insensitive to its depletion. Strikingly, loss of cyclophilin A (CypA) completely abolished HIV-1 dependence on POM121, whereas depletion of CPSF6 produced only partial rescue, demonstrating that POM121 sensitivity is dictated by the broader network of capsid-host interactions. Finally, POM121 depletion impaired HIV-1 nuclear accumulation and selectively disrupted the nuclear import of other viral and cellular cargo. Together, these findings identify POM121 as a selective regulator of lentiviral nuclear entry whose functional contribution is determined by capsid and host-factor context.

papers.title: Avian reovirus triggered ferroptosis, modulated lipid metabolism, and induced lipid droplet formation in infected cells, which was mediated in part by the p10/FAST protein
papers.abstract: In this study, we evaluated how avian reovirus (ARV) affected lipid metabolism and lipid droplets (LDs) in cell culture. ARV infection of chicken LMH cells significantly increased the size and number of LDs, however, LDs did not co-localize with virus factories, and neither overexpression by treatment with fatty acids (FAs), nor inhibition by treatment with TOFA or DGAT inhibitors significantly affected ARV replication. Lipidomic analysis revealed that following infection, total cellular lipid content increased approximately 25-fold, phosphatidylcholine (PC) content increased from 23.5 to 57.9%, and the polyunsaturated FA:monounsaturated FA ratio (PUFA:MUFA) decreased in membrane phospholipids but increased in triglycerides. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that there was also a reduction in the expression of genes involved in PUFA synthesis. As membrane PUFAs are susceptible to peroxidation, we investigated whether ARV induced ferroptosis. Consistent with this, ARV led to an increase in oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation that was partially iron dependent, and we found evidence that ferroptosis was proviral. Moreover, as ARV is known to form syncytia, we hypothesized that our observations were also the result of plasma membrane remodeling. Consistent with this, cells transfected with the ARV fusogenic p10/FAST protein formed syncytia, had a significantly upregulated number of LDs, and displayed hallmarks of ferroptosis. Taken together, we hypothesize that ARV induces syncytium formation and ferroptosis to facilitate viral spread to neighboring cells, but to prevent premature cell death due to these processes, lipid metabolism is modulated by infection, leading to an increase in LDs.

papers.title: Hepadnavirus tropism determined by diversified NTCP functionality in Feline species
papers.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exhibits a narrow host range, largely determined by sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptides (NTCP), a hepatic bile acid transporter acting as the HBV receptor. NTCP among animals appears to have evolved following trade-off mutations to lose its viral receptor activity while preserving its transporter function. Here, through profiling of the NTCP homologs from 23 mammalian species, we uncover unexpected functional heterogeneity of feline NTCPs. NTCPs derived from cat, tiger, and leopard supported viral preS1 binding and HBV infection, whereas lion-NTCP was deficient for preS1 binding and, notably, exhibited markedly reduced bile acid transport. Cat-NTCP was further demonstrated to have viral receptor function by productive infection in primary cat hepatocytes. Experimental mutagenesis identified double substitution at positions 191 and 268 as key determinants: introducing lion-type substitutions into cat-NTCP (G191R and T268A) abolished preS1 binding, whereas reciprocal substitutions in lion-NTCP restored receptor function. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that lion-NTCP adopts conformation in which a transmembrane helix bending enlarges the whole bile acid tunnel and disrupts preS1 compatibility. Such differences also determined host susceptibility to another feline-infected domestic cat HBV. These findings reveal diversified NTCP functionality with evolutionary plasticity that acquires resistance to hepadnavirus infection at the expense of physiological transporter function.

papers.title: Desiccation stress enhances virulence potential of group B Streptococcus
papers.abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) asymptomatically inhabits the gastrointestinal and female reproductive tracts but can also cause invasive diseases in susceptible individuals. Despite its clinical importance, relatively little is known about its ability to survive outside the host and whether environmental persistence contributes to transmission and infection. Here we investigate the GBS survival under nutrient starvation and desiccation, characterizing phenotypic and genomic adaptations associated with environmental persistence. GBS remained viable for 30 days during starvation at room temperature and for more than 80 days under desiccated conditions, with GBS grown to stationary-phase bacteria exhibiting greater survival than actively growing bacteria. Survival under desiccation was conserved among several clinically relevant GBS serotypes. Following rehydration desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced biofilm formation compared to control non-desiccated strains. Whole-genome sequencing identified mutations in genes involved in capsule biosynthesis, cell-envelope homeostasis, nutrient transport, and carbohydrate metabolism, suggesting that multiple adaptive pathways may contribute to environmental persistence. Importantly, desiccated GBS retained the capacity to colonize the vaginal mucosa and displayed increased invasion of reproductive tissues in a murine vaginal colonization model. In a systemic infection model, desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced virulence compared to control non-desiccated GBS, demonstrating that environmental survival does not diminish pathogenic potential. This environmental persistence may represent an underappreciated factor contributing to GBS transmission and the epidemiology of late-onset neonatal disease.

papers.title: Elevational variation in gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential across three Himalayan redstart species
papers.abstract: Environmental gradients and seasonal migration may influence host-associated microbial communities, yet their contributions to gut microbiome variation in montane birds remain poorly understood. We investigated gut microbial communities across 1,300 to 4,200 m in three Himalayan redstarts (Phoenicurus fuliginosus, P. leucocephalus, and P. frontalis) exhibiting contrasting seasonal movement strategies. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 46 fecal samples, we characterized microbial diversity, community composition, distance decay relationships, co-occurrence networks, and predicted functional potential. Elevation was significantly associated with microbial community composition, explaining approximately 3% of variation, whereas host species showed no significant association after accounting for elevation. P. fuliginosus exhibited significant compositional differences among most sampled elevations, whereas P. leucocephalus showed significant positive distance decay relationships. Alpha diversity showed no consistent elevational trend, while core microbial taxa and co-occurrence networks varied among elevational groups. PICRUSt2 analyses identified 28 predicted KEGG Level 3 pathways differing significantly among elevations, including pathways associated with amino acid, lipid, glycan, carbohydrate, and bile acid metabolism. Together, these findings highlight elevation as a significant correlate of gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential, with distinct patterns of microbial turnover among closely related Himalayan redstarts.

papers.title: Distinct binding modes shape exploitable asymmetries between echinocandin and triterpenoid resistance landscapes in Fks1
papers.abstract: Echinocandins are the first-line treatment for invasive fungal infections and work by inhibiting the fungal {beta}-1,3-glucan synthase Fks1. Recently, a first-in-class triterpenoid Fks1 inhibitor, ibrexafungerp, was approved for clinical use. The extent to which the difference between these drug classes alters the landscape of resistance mutations in Fks1 is unknown. We used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to quantify the effects of all single-amino-acid variants spanning 159 residues across the three canonical Fks1 resistance hotspots and flanking regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Drug selections revealed widespread position-specific cross-resistance and differential resistance, including an ibrexafungerp-specific resistance cluster downstream of hotspot 2 that defines a novel triterpenoid-specific resistance hotspot. We defined this as hotspot 4 and redefined the boundaries of the remaining three canonical echinocandin hotspots, based on the mutational landscape of our DMS analyses. Susceptibility testing of individual FKS1 variants of S. cerevisiae and Candidozyma auris strains confirmed conserved class-specific and cross-resistance patterns. Structure-guided ligand placement, molecular dynamics-based simulated annealing, and DMS-informed pose selection linked drug-specific phenotypes to distinct interaction networks, providing a molecular rationale for the observed differential resistance patterns. These data provide a framework for predicting antifungal resistance, informing treatment strategies and future drug design.

papers.title: A ribosome-dependent small-ORF switch controls flagellar gene expression and virulence
papers.abstract: RNA structures are active regulators of bacterial translation. Here, we identified a naturally occurring translation-enhancing small open reading frame (tesORF) that controls the expression of the flagellar operon fliFGHIJK in Salmonella enterica and other motile Enterobacterales. Nucleotide-resolution ribosome profiling revealed this previously unannotated 54-nucleotide ORF immediately upstream of fliF. Genetic, transcriptomic, and biochemical analyses support a model in which tesORF translation counteracts an inhibitory RNA structure, exposing the fliF ribosome-binding site and promoting translation initiation independently of the encoded peptide sequence. Disruption of tesORF translation reduced expression of the downstream operon and impaired motility and virulence-associated phenotypes in Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Yersinia. Together, our findings reveal how translation of a conserved small ORF regulates an entire flagellar operon through RNA structural remodelling, with consequences expending to the wider flagellar regulon, linking RNA structural dynamics to bacterial motility and virulence.

papers.title: Necroptosis is a targetable driver of severe coronavirus pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Human-pathogenic coronaviruses differ dramatically in pathogenicity but the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that highly pathogenic coronaviruses trigger necroptosis in the infected cells and lung tissues, whereas necroptosis is not detected in cells infected by seasonal coronavirus. Mechanistically, highly pathogenic coronaviruses produce Z-RNA, activate ZBP1 and initiates necroptotic cell death signaling, triggering necroinflammation and lung injury. In contrast, seasonal coronaviruses produce little to no Z-RNA, and do not activate necroptosis. Importantly, small-molecule inhibition of necroptosis attenuates inflammatory cytokine expression and markedly ameliorates lung damage in mice infected with all three highly pathogenic coronaviruses, independent of virus clearance. Overall, our study identifies necroptosis as a dominant mediator of coronavirus pathogenesis, and positions necroptosis blockade as a new therapeutic target against severe coronavirus diseases.

papers.title: Herbivore and carnivore microbial signatures indicate diet and health variation in human gut microbiota
papers.abstract: Diet is a key factor shaping gut microbiota in mammals, with herbivores and carnivores harboring distinct microbial communities. However, despite humans being highly omnivorous, it remains unclear whether their gut microbiota more closely resembles that of herbivores or carnivores or how individual-level variations along this spectrum are associated with human health status. We compared gut microbiota profiles of 858 samples from 109 mammalian species and constructed a Herbivore-Carnivore (HC) index based on bacterial groups characteristic of each diet. The HC-index positioned humans between herbivores and carnivores and showed that traditional hunter-gatherers and nonhuman apes retained herbivore-leaning profiles, whereas urbanized humans exhibited a shift toward a carnivore-leaning state. By applying the HC-index to >72,000 participants across multiple cohorts worldwide, we found that elevated HC-index values were associated with plant-based and fiber-rich diets, greater microbial diversity, enhanced potential to degrade plant-derived carbohydrates, favorable clinical measures, and lower prevalence of self-reported disease. We demonstrated that the HC balance of gut microbiota captures a conserved diet-related gradient across mammals and provides an interpretable framework linking human diet, microbial function, and health.

papers.title: Establishment of split-TurboID in Plasmodium falciparum facilitates identification of a PfAlba2 protein interaction network during late blood stage development
papers.abstract: Malaria parasites of the genus Plasmodium undergo complex multi-host lifecycles that require precise regulation of gene expression. Unlike model eukaryotes, Plasmodium spp. genomically encodes a limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators, but possess a substantial complement of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), highlighting the importance of post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms in regulating parasite gene expression. Among these RBPs are a family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins termed 'Alba' (acetylation lowers binding affinity) of which six have so far been identified in these parasites. Here, we investigated the localisation, functional importance and molecular associations of P. falciparum Alba protein PfAlba2 using two different endogenously tagged parasite lines. Using a GFP-FKBP tagged line, we demonstrated that PfAlba2 is expressed throughout asexual blood stage development and primarily localised in the cytosol. Conditional mislocalisation experiments indicated that PfAlba2 contributes to normal parasite growth. To overcome challenges in generating a miniTurboID proximity labelling line, we established a custom split-TurboID proximity labelling system for use in P. falciparum to characterise the PfAlba2 proxiome during asexual blood stage development. The split-TurboID system facilitated identification of 101 enriched PfAlba2 proximal proteins in schizont stage development, with significant enrichment for proteins involved in translation initiation, including two additional Alba family members, PfAlba1 and PfAlba4. Complementary RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 380 PfAlba2-associated transcripts with significant enrichments including cytosolic ribosomes, rRNA-processing factors, PfAlba1, and egress and invasion-related transcripts (PfRALP1, PfRON4, PfRH1, PfRH5). Together, these findings implicate PfAlba2 in RNA metabolism and translational regulation, suggesting an important regulatory function for this protein during parasite blood stage development.

papers.title: A Xenopus laevis Model for Systemic Fungal Infections
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis possesses both innate and adaptive immune systems, and we previously demonstrated its utility as an infection model for human bacterial pathogens. In this study, we investigated the utility of X. laevis as a model for fungal infections. The human-pathogenic fungi Candida albicans and Aspergillus fumigatus exhibited greater lethality in X. laevis than the nonpathogenic fungi Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe. In frogs infected with C. albicans, viable fungal cells were detected in the blood and multiple organs early after infection, and gross white lesions and fungal hyphae were observed in the kidneys. C. albicans infection also increased renal expression of the proinflammatory cytokine gene s tnf and il1b, as well as the tissue injury-associated gene clu. Treatment with the antifungal agents amphotericin B and micafungin significantly improved the survival of C. albicans-infected frogs. Furthermore, a homozygous deletion mutant of UME6, a gene associated with C. albicans virulence, exhibited reduced lethality compared with the wild-type strain. These findings establish X. laevis as a vertebrate model of systemic fungal infection that enables the evaluation of fungal virulence, host responses, and the therapeutic efficacy of antifungal agents.

papers.title: Functional characterisation and identification of a core interactome of Plasmodium regulatory protein Alba4
papers.abstract: Plasmodium spp. parasites have complex lifecycles that rely on strict regulation of gene and protein expression. Current evidence suggests that P. falciparum has a relatively limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators and RNA interference (RNAi)-associated small RNAs compared to model eukaryotes, potentially reflecting a greater reliance on RNA binding protein (RBP)-mediated post-transcriptional regulation (PTR). Among these RBPs, the acetylation lowers binding affinity (Alba) family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins has been implicated in RNA metabolism and regulation of mRNA stability and translation. In Plasmodium spp. parasites, the Alba family has expanded to include up to six members, with sequence divergence and structural modifications beyond the conserved Alba domain leading to diversification of family members, some of which appear restricted to Plasmodium and related parasites. In this study, we were unable to truncate PfAlba4, but successfully generated an endogenously tagged PfAlba4 parasite line, representing the first successful instance of endogenous tagging of a PfAlba family protein. Utilising this transgenic line, we confirm ubiquitous expression throughout blood stage development and its predominantly cytosolic localisation. Conditional loss of PfAlba4 through the knock-sideways approach demonstrated an important role for PfAlba4 in blood stage development and proteomics analysis defined a protein interaction network of 67 significantly enriched proteins, with notable enrichment of proteins potentially involved in RNA processing and regulation. Further characterisation of one of these proteins, the uncharacterised protein PF3D7_0706500, revealed a partially overlapping network of proximal proteins enriched for RNA-regulatory factors, suggesting potentially shared roles in PTR. RNA Immunoprecipitation-Sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 692 PfAlba4 associated transcripts, with an enrichment of a pyrimidine-rich motif in their 3' untranslated regions, suggesting a potential sequence-dependent mechanism of RNA recognition. Integration of proteomic and RIP-Seq datasets in late blood stage parasites revealed a consistent association with RNA processing and regulatory pathways, implicating PfAlba4 in post-transcriptional regulation. Together these findings establish PfAlba4 as an important component of the RNA-regulatory landscape in P. falciparum and highlight the importance of PfAlba proteins for malaria parasite blood stage development.

papers.title: NON-NUCLEOSIDE REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE INHIBITORS BLOCK THE INCORPORATION OF VIRAL GLYCOPROTEINS INTO HIV-1 VIRIONS
papers.abstract: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) are a key component of antiretroviral therapy that block reverse transcription in newly infected cells. NNRTIs have also been reported to induce premature activation of the HIV-1 protease in virus-producing cells, an activity that has been optimized in a class of NNRTIs known as targeted activators of cell kill (TACK). In this study, we used the TACK compound Pyr01 to investigate how NNRTI-induced premature protease activation affects virion composition and infectivity. We found that Pyr01 treatment markedly reduces the incorporation of the HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycoprotein into virus particles in an Env cytoplasmic tail-independent manner. Pyr01 treatment also disrupts the virion incorporation of foreign viral glycoproteins and causes a substantial loss of the viral enzymes from virions. Virions produced from NNRTI-treated cells exhibit reduced membrane order. The defect in viral glycoprotein incorporation requires an active protease, implicating premature protease-mediated disruption of the Gag lattice and resulting changes in membrane properties as the primary mechanism underlying these effects. These findings reveal that NNRTI-induced premature protease activation during virus assembly fundamentally changes the protein composition and membrane order of HIV-1 virions to markedly reduce particle infectivity. These results have implications for the use of TACK compounds therapeutically and provide basic insights into the properties of the viral membrane that promote viral glycoprotein incorporation.

papers.title: Heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 Attenuates Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Intestinal Inflammation and Barrier Disruption
papers.abstract: Intestinal barrier dysfunction and excessive inflammation contribute to the pathogenesis of various metabolic and gastrointestinal diseases. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces systemic and intestinal inflammation, disrupts epithelial tight junctions, and impairs intestinal barrier integrity. Although heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 exhibits antiviral activity, its effects on intestinal barrier function remain unclear. In this study, we examined whether heat-killed D279 preserves intestinal barrier integrity and attenuates LPS-induced inflammatory responses in vivo (LPS-challenged mice), ex vivo (mouse peritoneal macrophages), and in vitro (IEC-6 intestinal epithelial cells). Cytokine and receptor gene expression in macrophages was measured to evaluate inflammatory responses. Furthermore, barrier function was assessed using transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and the expression of tight junction-related genes was assessed. D279 alleviated LPS-induced intestinal injury in LPS-challenged mice, as indicated by the attenuation of colon shortening and histopathological changes compared to those in the LPS control group. In peritoneal macrophages, D279 pretreatment suppressed LPS-induced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-, IL-1{beta}, and IL-12{beta}), increased IL-10 expression, and reduced LPS-induced upregulation of MLCK expression. This postbiotic increased basal cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner in IEC-6 cells. Moreover, it enhanced epithelial barrier development (increased TEER) and upregulated tight junction gene expression. These findings demonstrate that heat-killed D279 primarily confers its benefits by attenuating LPS-induced cytokine responses, limiting the upregulation of MLCK expression, and partially preserving goblet cell abundance. This is consistent with its protective postbiotic role in intestinal homeostasis. Thus, this study introduces a candidate postbiotic for the promotion of intestinal resilience under systemic inflammatory stress.

papers.title: Sphingolipid Hydroxylation Governs Fungal Pathogenicity and Drug Susceptibility: Scs7 as a Druggable Target in Candida albicans
papers.abstract: Sphingolipids are essential structural components of the fungal plasma membrane and key signaling hubs that orchestrate pathogenicity. While both fungi and mammals perform sphingolipid hydroxylation, they rely on evolutionarily divergent enzymatic systems, establishing a biochemical divergence exploitable for selective targeting. Here, through a screening of sphingolipid metabolic genes, we identify the sphingolipid -hydroxylase Scs7 as a central regulator of membrane homeostasis, virulence, and caspofungin susceptibility in Candida albicans. Genetic ablation of SCS7 depletes hydroxylated sphingolipids, disrupts memberane organization, and compromises cell wall integrity, which collectively impair hyphal morphogenesis, biofilm formation, and stress tolerance through blockade of the cAMP-PKA signaling axis. In a murine cutaneous infection model, SCS7 deletion markedly attenuates fungal burden, hyperinflammation, and epidermal barrier disruption, underscoring its non-redundant role in host-pathogen interaction. Leveraging the fungus-specific architecture of Scs7, we performed virtual screening and identified resveratrol as a natural Scs7 inhibitor. Resveratrol recapitulates the lipidomic and phenotypic defects of SCS7 deletion and synergizes with caspofungin to enhance fungal killing. Our study establishes sphingolipid -hydroxylation as a master determinant of fungal membrane fitness and validates Scs7 as a promising, fungus-specific antifungal target with dual anti-virulence and chemosensitizing activities.
